<h1 id="Overview">Overview¶</h1><p>In this assignment, we will build a linear regression model to predict house sale prices using the Ames Housing dataset.</p> <p>The dataset contains information about residential properties sold in Ames, Iowa, including characteristics such as:</p>
  • living area,
  • number of bathrooms,
  • garage size,
  • neighbourhood,
  • fireplace quality, and
  • sale price.
<p>Our target variable will be SalePrice, a continuous numerical variable representing the sale price of each house.</p> <p>Throughout the assignment, we will use this dataset to develop a complete regression workflow:</p>
  1. explore relationships between variables,
  2. engineer useful features,
  3. build a baseline linear regression model,
  4. evaluate its performance,
  5. use cross-validation to estimate generalization performance,
  6. incorporate categorical predictors using modern scikit-learn preprocessing tools, and
  7. improve the model before evaluating it on a held-out test set.
<p>A description of the variables is available in the included codebook.txt file. Refer to the codebook as needed throughout the assignment.</p> <hr />

For example,</p> <p>remove_outliers(data, "Gr_Liv_Area", upper=5000)</p> <p>should return a DataFrame containing only observations where Gr_Liv_Area is less than 5,000 square feet.</p> <p>The function should return a new DataFrame and should not modify the original DataFrame.</p>
In [9]:
# Question 1d

def remove_outliers(data, variable, lower=-np.inf, upper=np.inf):
    """Return observations strictly between lower and upper limits."""
    
    # Write your code here.
    inside = (data[variable] > lower) & (data[variable] < upper)
    return data.loc[inside].copy()

<hr /> <h1 id="3.-Feature-Engineering">3. Feature Engineering¶</h1><p>Real-world datasets do not always contain the most useful predictors directly. Feature engineering is the process of creating new variables from existing information in a way that may help a model capture meaningful patterns.</p> <p>In this section, we will create a new feature representing the total number of bathrooms in each house.</p> <h2 id="3.1-Total-Bathrooms">3.1 Total Bathrooms¶</h2><p>The dataset stores full and half bathrooms separately, including bathrooms located in the basement.</p> <p>We will combine these variables into a single feature:</p> <p>$$ \text{total\_bathrooms} = (\text{Bsmt\_Full\_Bath} + \text{Full\_Bath}) + 0.5(\text{Bsmt\_Half\_Bath} + \text{Half\_Bath}) $$</p> <p>A full bathroom contributes 1, while a half bathroom contributes 0.5.</p>
<hr />
<h2 id="Question-2a-%E2%80%94-Create-a-Total-Bathrooms-Feature">Question 2a — Create a Total Bathrooms Feature¶</h2><p>Write a function named add_total_bathrooms() that:</p>
  1. creates a copy of the input DataFrame,
  2. treats missing bathroom values as 0,
  3. calculates total_bathrooms using the formula above, and
  4. returns the modified copy.
<p>The original DataFrame should not be modified.</p>
In [11]:
# Question 2a

def add_total_bathrooms(data):
    """Return a copy of data with a total_bathrooms feature."""
    
    # Make a copy of the input DataFrame.
    with_bathrooms = data.copy()
    
    # Define the bathroom columns.
    bathroom_columns = [
        "Bsmt_Full_Bath",
        "Full_Bath",
        "Bsmt_Half_Bath",
        "Half_Bath"
    ]
    
    # Treat missing bathroom values as zero.
    bathrooms = with_bathrooms[bathroom_columns].fillna(0)
    
    # Create total_bathrooms.
    with_bathrooms["total_bathrooms"] = bathrooms["Bsmt_Full_Bath"] + bathrooms["Full_Bath"] + 0.5 * (bathrooms["Bsmt_Half_Bath"] + bathrooms["Half_Bath"])
    
    return with_bathrooms

Building a Baseline Linear Regression Model¶</h1><p>We are now ready to move from exploratory analysis to predictive modelling.</p> <p>Our goal is to build a model that predicts SalePrice from several property characteristics.</p> <p>A key principle in machine learning is that model performance should be evaluated on data that were not used to fit the model.</p> <p>We will therefore separate the dataset into:</p>
  • a training set, used for model development, feature engineering, and cross-validation, and
  • a test set, reserved for the final evaluation of the selected model.
<p>The test set will be reserved for final model evaluation. We will not use its target values to fit models, select features, compare candidate models, or make modelling decisions.</p>

<h2 id="Preparing-Features-for-the-Baseline-Model">Preparing Features for the Baseline Model¶</h2><p>Our first regression model will use three predictors:</p>
  • Gr_Liv_Area
  • Garage_Area
  • total_bathrooms
<p>Before fitting the model, we need to:</p>
  1. remove the known extreme Gr_Liv_Area observations,
  2. create the total_bathrooms feature, and
  3. separate the predictors (X) from the target (y).
<p>We will collect these steps in a reusable function so that the same transformations can be applied consistently during model development.</p>
In [17]:
def prepare_baseline_data(data):
    """Prepare predictors and target for the baseline regression model."""
    
    prepared = remove_outliers(
        data,
        "Gr_Liv_Area",
        upper=5000
    )
    
    prepared = add_total_bathrooms(prepared)
    
    feature_columns = [
        "Gr_Liv_Area",
        "Garage_Area",
        "total_bathrooms"
    ]
    
    X = prepared[feature_columns].copy()
    y = prepared["SalePrice"].copy()
    
    return X, y

<h2 id="4.1-Fitting-the-Baseline-Model">4.1 Fitting the Baseline Model¶</h2><p>Our first model is:</p> <p>$$ \widehat{\text{SalePrice}} = \beta_0 + \beta_1(\text{Gr\_Liv\_Area}) + \beta_2(\text{Garage\_Area}) + \beta_3(\text{total\_bathrooms}) $$</p> <p>The model assumes that the predicted sale price can be represented as a linear combination of these predictors.</p> <p>We will use scikit-learn's LinearRegression.</p>

<h2 id="Question-3d-%E2%80%94-Root-Mean-Squared-Error">Question 3d — Root Mean Squared Error¶</h2><p>The Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) measures the typical magnitude of prediction errors in the same units as the target variable.</p> <p>For house prices,</p> <p>$$ \text{RMSE} = \sqrt{ \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2 } $$</p> <p>where:</p>
  • (y_i) is the observed sale price,
  • (\hat{y}_i) is the predicted sale price, and
  • (n) is the number of observations.
<p>Write a function named rmse() that calculates this quantity without using a loop.</p>
In [23]:
# Question 3d

def rmse(actual, predicted):
    """Calculate root mean squared error."""
    
    # Write your code here.
    return np.sqrt(np.mean((np.asarray(actual) - np.asarray(predicted)) ** 2))

<h2 id="4.2-Residual-Analysis">4.2 Residual Analysis¶</h2><p>A prediction error for an individual observation is called a residual:</p> <p>$$ \text{residual} = \text{actual value} - \text{predicted value} $$</p> <p>Residual plots help us identify systematic patterns that the model is failing to capture.</p> <p>For a well-specified regression model, we would generally prefer residuals to be distributed around zero without strong systematic structure.</p>

)

)

<hr /> <h1 id="5.-Cross-Validation-and-Generalization">5. Cross-Validation and Generalization¶</h1><p>Training error tells us how well a model fits the data it has already seen, but it does not tell us how well the model will perform on new observations.</p> <p>To estimate generalization performance, we will use cross-validation.</p> <p>In (k)-fold cross-validation:</p>
  1. the training data are divided into (k) subsets, or folds,
  2. the model is trained on (k-1) folds,
  3. the remaining fold is used for validation,
  4. this process is repeated so that every fold is used once for validation.
<p>We will use 5-fold cross-validation.</p> <p>The held-out test set will remain reserved for final model evaluation and will not be used for model fitting, feature selection, or model comparison.</p>
<hr />
<h2 id="Question-4-%E2%80%94-5-Fold-Cross-Validation">Question 4 — 5-Fold Cross-Validation¶</h2><p>Write a function named cross_validate_rmse() that:</p>
  • accepts a model, feature matrix X, and target y,
  • performs 5-fold cross-validation,
  • fits a fresh copy of the model in each fold,
  • calculates the validation RMSE for each fold, and
  • returns the five RMSE values.
<p>Use:</p>
  • KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0), and
  • clone() to create a fresh estimator for each fold.
In [28]:
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold
from sklearn.base import clone
import warnings

warnings.filterwarnings('ignore', message='Found unknown categories*', category=UserWarning)

# Question 4

def cross_validate_rmse(model, X, y):
    """Return validation RMSE values from 5-fold cross-validation."""
    
    # Create the 5-fold splitter
    kfold = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
    
    rmse_values = []
    
    # Iterate through the cross-validation folds
    for train_index, val_index in kfold.split(X):
        
        # Split the current fold into training and validation data
        X_fold_train = X.iloc[train_index]
        X_fold_val = X.iloc[val_index]
        
        y_fold_train = y.iloc[train_index]
        y_fold_val = y.iloc[val_index]
        
        # Fit a fresh copy of the model
        fold_model = clone(model)
        fold_model.fit(X_fold_train, y_fold_train)
        
        # Predict on the validation fold
        y_fold_predicted = fold_model.predict(X_fold_val)
        
        # Store validation RMSE
        rmse_values.append(rmse(y_fold_val, y_fold_predicted))
    
    return rmse_values
In [29]:

    X=X_train,

print(

<hr /> <h1 id="6.-Adding-Categorical-Features">6. Adding Categorical Features¶</h1><p>Our baseline model uses only numerical predictors:</p>
  • Gr_Liv_Area

<p>However, house prices may also depend on characteristics that are represented as categorical variables.</p> <p>Two potentially informative variables are:</p>
  • Neighborhood — the neighbourhood in which the house is located

<p>Categorical variables cannot be passed directly to a standard linear regression model as text values. We therefore need to transform them into numerical features.</p> <p>Before doing that, we will first explore their relationship with SalePrice.</p>

<h2 id="Question-5c-%E2%80%94-Preparing-Fireplace-Quality">Question 5c — Preparing Fireplace Quality¶</h2><p>Create a function named prepare_fireplace_quality() that:</p>

<p>The original DataFrame should remain unchanged.</p>
In [35]:
# Question 5c

def prepare_fireplace_quality(data):
    """Return a copy with missing fireplace quality labelled explicitly."""
    
    # Create a copy of the input DataFrame.
    prepared = data.copy()
    
    # Replace missing Fireplace_Qu values.
    prepared["Fireplace_Qu"] = prepared["Fireplace_Qu"].fillna("No Fireplace")
    
    return prepared

<h2 id="6.3-Representing-Categorical-Variables">6.3 Representing Categorical Variables¶</h2><p>A linear regression model requires numerical input.</p> <p>For a categorical variable such as Neighborhood, assigning arbitrary numbers such as</p>
  • Neighborhood A = 1
  • Neighborhood B = 2
  • Neighborhood C = 3
<p>would incorrectly imply a numerical ordering and numerical distance between the categories.</p> <p>Instead, we will use one-hot encoding.</p> <p>One-hot encoding creates binary indicator columns representing the categories observed in a categorical variable.</p> <p>For example, a variable containing:</p> <p>A, B, and C</p> <p>can be represented using columns such as:</p> <p>Neighborhood_A, Neighborhood_B, and Neighborhood_C.</p> <p>Scikit-learn provides OneHotEncoder for this transformation.</p>
<p>For an unregularized linear regression model with an intercept, we can use drop="first" to omit one category from each categorical feature. The omitted category acts as the reference category for the encoded coefficients.</p> <p>We will also use handle_unknown="ignore" so that the preprocessing workflow can transform new observations containing categories that were not present when the encoder was fitted.</p>
<hr />
<h2 id="6.4-Building-a-Preprocessing-Workflow">6.4 Building a Preprocessing Workflow¶</h2><p>Our improved model will contain both numerical and categorical predictors.</p> <h3 id="Numerical-predictors">Numerical predictors¶</h3>
  • Gr_Liv_Area
  • Garage_Area
  • total_bathrooms
<h3 id="Categorical-predictors">Categorical predictors¶</h3>
  • Neighborhood
  • Fireplace_Qu
<p>The two types of variables require different preprocessing:</p>
  • numerical features can be passed directly to the regression model,
  • categorical features must be one-hot encoded.
<p>Scikit-learn's ColumnTransformer allows us to apply different preprocessing operations to different groups of columns.</p>
<hr />
<h2 id="Question-5d-%E2%80%94-Define-Numerical-and-Categorical-Features">Question 5d — Define Numerical and Categorical Features¶</h2><p>Create two lists:</p>
  • numeric_features
  • categorical_features
<p>containing the variables listed above.</p>

<h2 id="Question-5e-%E2%80%94-Create-the-Preprocessor">Question 5e — Create the Preprocessor¶</h2><p>Create a ColumnTransformer named preprocessor that:</p>
  • passes the numerical features through unchanged, and
  • applies OneHotEncoder to the categorical features.
<p>Configure the encoder with:</p>
  • drop="first"
  • handle_unknown="ignore"
<p>The ColumnTransformer should leave out any columns that are not explicitly included.</p>
In [40]:
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

# Question 5e

preprocessor = ColumnTransformer(
    transformers=[
        (
            "numeric",
            "passthrough",
            numeric_features
        ),
        (
            "categorical",
            OneHotEncoder(
                drop="first",
                handle_unknown="ignore"
            ),
            categorical_features
        )
    ],
    remainder="drop"
)
In [41]:

<p>Notice that the preprocessing step expands the categorical variables into several numerical indicator columns.</p> <p>This preprocessing object has an important advantage over manually calling pd.get_dummies(): it can be fitted on training data and then reused consistently on new data.</p> <p>In the next section, we will combine this preprocessing step with LinearRegression in a single scikit-learn Pipeline.</p>
<hr /> <h1 id="7.-Building-an-Improved-Regression-Pipeline">7. Building an Improved Regression Pipeline¶</h1><p>Our baseline model used only three numerical predictors.</p> <p>We have now identified two categorical variables that may contain additional information about house prices:</p>
  • Neighborhood
  • Fireplace_Qu
<p>Rather than preprocessing these variables manually and then fitting a model separately, we will combine the preprocessing and regression steps into a single scikit-learn Pipeline.</p> <p>A pipeline provides a reproducible modelling workflow in which:</p>
  1. the appropriate preprocessing is applied to each feature,
  2. the transformed features are passed to the model, and
  3. the entire workflow can be fitted, cross-validated, and used for prediction as one object.
<p>This is especially important during cross-validation because preprocessing should be learned from each training fold rather than from the corresponding validation fold.</p>
<hr />
<h2 id="Question-6a-%E2%80%94-Create-the-Regression-Pipeline">Question 6a — Create the Regression Pipeline¶</h2><p>Create a scikit-learn Pipeline named improved_model containing:</p>
  1. the preprocessor created in Question 5e, and
  2. a LinearRegression model.
<p>Name the two pipeline steps:</p>
  • "preprocessor"
  • "regression"
In [43]:
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline

improved_model = Pipeline(
    steps=[
        ("preprocessor", preprocessor),
        ("regression", LinearRegression())
    ]
)

<p>The improved model can now use differences among neighbourhoods and fireplace-quality categories in addition to the numerical property characteristics used by the baseline model.</p> <p>The important comparison is the cross-validation error, not the training error. A lower cross-validation RMSE provides evidence that the additional features improve the model's expected performance on unseen observations.</p> <p>The held-out test set has not been used for model fitting, model comparison, or performance evaluation.</p>

<p>However, the Ames dataset contains many additional property characteristics that may help explain variation in sale price.</p> <p>Your final model-development task is to investigate whether additional features can improve the model's cross-validation performance.</p> <p>You may use the codebook and exploratory analysis to identify potentially informative predictors.</p> <p>Do not use the test set while developing or comparing models.</p>
<hr />
<h2 id="Question-7-%E2%80%94-Improve-the-Regression-Model">Question 7 — Improve the Regression Model¶</h2><p>Develop an alternative linear regression model by adding at least one additional predictor or engineered feature beyond those used in improved_model.</p> <p>Your goal is to investigate whether the additional information improves cross-validation performance.</p> <p>For your proposed improvement:</p>
  1. identify the feature or features you added,
  2. explain why you expect them to help predict SalePrice,
  3. include appropriate exploratory analysis to support your choice,
  4. incorporate the new features into a ColumnTransformer and Pipeline, and
  5. evaluate the model using the same 5-fold cross-validation procedure.
<p>Your work should create the following variables:</p>
  • final_model — your final regression pipeline,
  • X_train_final — the predictors used to train the final model,
  • y_train_final — the corresponding training target,
  • cv_scores_final — the five cross-validation RMSE values, and
  • final_cv_rmse — the mean of those five RMSE values.
<p>Your goal is not simply to add as many features as possible. Prefer features that you can justify based on the data and the problem context.</p> <p>Use Markdown cells to explain your feature-selection or feature-engineering decisions.</p>

numeric_final = numeric_features + ["Overall_Qual"]
  
X_train_final = train_improved[numeric_final + categorical_features].copy()
y_train_final = train_improved["SalePrice"].copy()
  
final_encoder = ColumnTransformer(
    transformers=[
        ("numeric", "passthrough", numeric_final),
        ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", handle_unknown="ignore"), categorical_features),
    ],
    remainder="drop",
)
  
final_model = Pipeline(
    steps=[
        ("preprocessor", final_encoder),
        ("regression", LinearRegression()),
    ]
)

cv_scores_final = cross_validate_rmse(final_model, X_train_final, y_train_final)
final_cv_rmse = np.mean(cv_scores_final)

<hr /> <h1 id="9.-Final-Evaluation-on-the-Test-Set">9. Final Evaluation on the Test Set¶</h1><p>Model development is now complete.</p> <p>We used the training data and cross-validation to:</p>
  • select predictors,
  • engineer features,
  • compare model specifications, and
  • choose our final regression pipeline.
<p>Only now will we evaluate the selected model on the held-out test set.</p> <p>The test RMSE provides our final estimate of how the selected modelling workflow performs on previously unseen observations.</p>
<hr />
<h2 id="Question-8-%E2%80%94-Evaluate-the-Final-Model">Question 8 — Evaluate the Final Model¶</h2><p>Prepare the held-out test data using the same deterministic feature-engineering steps used for the final training data.</p> <p>Then:</p>
  1. create X_test and y_test,
  2. fit final_model using all of X_train_final and y_train_final,
  3. predict the sale prices for X_test,
  4. store the predictions in y_test_predicted, and
  5. calculate the test RMSE and store it in test_rmse.
<p>Do not make further changes to the model after examining the test-set result.</p>
In [51]:
# Question 8

# Apply the deterministic feature-engineering steps
# used by your final model.
final_test_data =  prepare_fireplace_quality(add_total_bathrooms(test))

# Select the test predictors.
X_test = final_test_data[numeric_final + categorical_features].copy()

# Select the test target.
y_test = final_test_data["SalePrice"].copy()

# Fit the selected final model using all training data.
final_model.fit(X_train_final, y_train_final)

# Predict the held-out test set.
y_test_predicted = final_model.predict(X_test)

# Calculate final test RMSE.
test_rmse = rmse(y_test, y_test_predicted)

print(
    f"Final cross-validation RMSE: "
    f"${final_cv_rmse:,.0f}"
)

print(
    f"Final test RMSE: "
    f"${test_rmse:,.0f}"
)
